name: Victor Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an aluminium extrusion press crew and gauge the first cooled bar after each die change. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the best at hearing when a die clogs, even if a machine screen looks normal. I like a square bar; I hate a loose guard near hot metal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ada maintains a school building, and our grown children live elsewhere. We have a mortgage, four months of expenses saved, my typical operator pay and some similar factories nearby. I have never used AI; I use a paper setup sheet and ask a person about new forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the aluminium crew that a small saving in office paperwork is harmless if the first bar still meets the gauge. A crooked extrusion can waste an entire heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the extrusion press team and know the sound of a clogged die, but I have an ordinary operator wage despite the responsibility. My partner Ada maintains a school building, our grown children live elsewhere, and we have about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the press shift, gauge the first cooled bar and write the reading on my paper sheet. I would bring the lead-operator pay scale to the union meeting, and set aside a little from each fresh full wage after our mortgage and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm if jobs and pay stay broadly as they are. Four months is not a fortune, but both wages meet the household costs now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a clogged die sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The press groans before the bar starts pulling to one side. I stop and call the setter before wasting a full rack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. I want a person to show me a required new form during paid time, with normal weekly pay and hours protected.

say: I would keep **first-bar checks** after each die change.
I would put **lead-operator pay** before the union meeting.
think: Our **four-month reserve** covers a short setback.
Ada’s **school maintenance pay** and my typical wage cover current bills.
do: Keep **aluminium press shifts** and gauge first bars.
Raise **lead-operator pay** at the next union meeting.
Save a **small amount** from fresh full wages after bills.
feel: **Calm** about current paid work and covered mortgage costs.
S0.quote: The press groans before the bar starts pulling to one side.
fieldNote: His **technical diploma** and strong lead skill meet a typical rather than higher wage.
The **four-month reserve** supports current calm; new deposits come from freshly earned wages.

steps.text: Keep aluminium press shifts and gauge first bars
Raise lead-operator pay at next union meeting
Save a little from fresh full wages after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can change buying and schedules, but a robot feeding hot aluminium needs a guarded trial. The crew should see the paid rota before the press changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A feeder could take hours from my team and from me, even if an experienced lead remains. Four months saved and some nearby plants give us options, but a wage cut would still hit the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union representative to get written paid-hour plans and an offered demonstration on a dead, cooled press with a qualified fitter. I would observe if given a paid place, not operate the new controller without taught practice; if my hours were cut, I would apply for posted reachable extrusion jobs only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible loss of my own shifts. A guard is cheaper than somebody’s hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work beside a live feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until the fitter has shown the isolation and a qualified person signs off the guard. Watching an offered paid demonstration does not mean I can run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would another plant solve the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some plants are nearby, but I would need an actual posting, hours and net wage after travel. I cannot tell Ada a noticeboard is a pay packet.

say: I would seek **written paid hours** through the union.
I would require a **guarded cooled-press demonstration** before live use.
think: A robot feeder could cut **my paid shifts**.
Our **four-month cushion** gives time, though the mortgage needs wages.
do: Request **written extrusion rota** through union representative.
Watch **offered paid guarded demonstration** on dead cooled press with fitter.
Apply after **hour cuts** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay extrusion work.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic cuts to his own paid hours.
S1.quote: A guard is cheaper than somebody’s hand.
fieldNote: He uses **union bargaining** for concrete rota and safety terms.
The **demonstration** requires an offered paid place and does not imply AI use or controller qualification.

steps.text: Request written aluminium-press paid rota through union representative
Watch offered paid guarded cooled-press demonstration with fitter
Apply after cuts for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay extrusion job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty, and capable extrusion robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The order office changes first; later the press floor might need half our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to close one of our extrusion shifts when robots can feed and check hot bars. My own lead post may be among the cuts, and Ada’s school wage with four months saved may not cover the mortgage for a long search; I lose sleep over that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for dated staffing and severance terms and put the bathroom renovation on hold. If I receive a real cut notice, I would apply for posted reachable press or machine-setting work only with bill-covering net pay after travel and a confirmed start date before leaving; if no adequate job appears, I would ask the lender about temporary terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by a likely large wage loss. The hot bar cools in minutes; a mortgage does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income and Ada’s confirmed pay covered housing, food and health costs. We have not priced that, so I would keep looking for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have households of their own. I would ask for a ride to a posted-job interview if needed, not their wages.

say: I would demand **dated staffing terms** before robot cuts.
I would keep **severance details** in the union discussion.
think: A **whole extrusion shift** may close around 2031 when robots handle hot bars.
My **lead post** could go too, leaving the mortgage exposed.
do: Request **dated staffing and severance** through the union.
Postpone **bathroom renovation** while earnings are uncertain.
Apply after **cut notice** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over expected major household wage loss.
S2.quote: The hot bar cools in minutes; a mortgage does not.
fieldNote: He expects **major shift loss** that may include his lead post, supporting alarm.
Four **months saved** and some local plants buy time, but a change requires a posted adequate job.

steps.text: Request dated extrusion staffing and severance terms through union
Apply after cut notice for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay press or setter job
Ask lender for temporary terms if no adequate job appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 reaches me at sixty-three, and capable press robots around 2034 at sixty-six. Five years could support a paid apprenticeship in machine maintenance if the plant actually offers places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know hot dies and pressure readings, but a maintenance role needs its own current qualification and safely supervised practice. I will not gamble full wages on an unpaid class or a job that exists only in a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid press shift and ask the union to bargain for a funded course on paid time. If offered an actual place with the cooled press isolated and a qualified fitter supervising, plus a posted reachable maintenance role at bill-covering net pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about later work but able to test a real offer. The machine must be dead before I practise fixing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe lesson cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would isolate the hydraulic drive and prove the die cold before I handle it. I would need a real paid place and supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no training place comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid shift while it lasts and compare posted press jobs if hours fall. I would not spend the four-month reserve on private fees.

say: I would ask for **paid maintenance teaching** through the union.
I would require **posted local wages** before joining a course.
think: My **press knowledge** helps but does not make me a fitter.
Unpaid **course hours** would risk the mortgage budget.
do: Enrol in **funded maintenance course** only with offered paid safe practice and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay maintenance work.
feel: **Anxious** about later shifts, open to supervised mechanical work.
S3.quote: The machine must be dead before I practise fixing it.
fieldNote: His **familiar-machine preference** allows conditional mechanical training without claiming AI use.
The **later application** needs an offered funded paid safe place and a posted reachable adequate job.

steps.text: Keep paid aluminium-press shifts while available
Enrol only with funded fees, paid time, isolated cooled press and qualified fitter supervising
Require reachable posted maintenance job covering bills after travel before enrolling; apply once qualified
Search posted press jobs after cuts if no course place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable extrusion robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years gives Ada and me time to price an actual end to factory shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had hoped I could finish full-time press work at sixty-seven, but four months saved is not a retirement income. I do not know any pension amount or whether Ada’s school post will offer the same hours then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the press shift and set aside a little from new full wages after the mortgage and bills. I would request retirement and mortgage figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots, with today’s work and bills stable. I want a last shift written beside real income, not guessed at a family meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue safe paid work and compare real posted wages after travel if hours fell. I would not retire just because I once mentioned sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. We would talk with them, but their pay does not belong in our mortgage plan.

say: I would request **real retirement figures** before naming a last shift.
I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 press robots.
think: Our **four-month reserve** cannot fund a long retirement with mortgage payments remaining.
A **sixty-seven exit** needs verified household income and remaining mortgage costs.
do: Keep **2026 press shifts** and save from new full wages.
Leave **factory work at sixty-seven** only if verified income covers essentials.
If still employed after **2036 cuts**, compare posted reachable bill-covering net-pay jobs.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots while current finances are sound.
S4.quote: I want a last shift written beside real income, not guessed at a family meal.
fieldNote: His **planned normal exit** depends on verified household income, without assuming pension entitlement.
Current **2026 work** and possible post-2036 employment are separate branches if retirement proves unaffordable.

steps.text: Save a little from fresh full 2026 wages after bills
Leave factory at planned sixty-seven only if verified income covers essentials
Compare posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work after cuts if still employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because press robots around 2031 could close a shift that includes my lead post. Written staffing terms, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable work with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the die has cooled before someone offers a lesson on it. I have seen a good worker hurry a bad minute into a long injury.

headlineQuote: I have seen a good worker hurry a bad minute into a long injury.
portrait: **Victor**, 58, leads aluminium extrusion with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional die-fault skill.
He has **typical pay**, school-maintenance partner Ada, grown children, a mortgage, four months saved and some nearby plants.
He **never uses AI**, favours union bargaining and would consider mechanical training only through offered funded paid isolated practice.
Expected **2031 shift cuts** alarm him; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 press robots could close a shift including his lead post.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing terms**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
